what_its_for: Digoxin is used to treat heart failure and certain irregular heartbeats (like atrial fibrillation). It helps your heart beat more slowly and steadily, and it helps your heart pump blood more efficiently throughout your body.
how_to_take: Take digoxin by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablets. Take it at the same time every day to keep a steady amount in your body. Do not take more or less than your doctor prescribed.
dosing: Your dose will be carefully set by your doctor based on your age, weight, kidney function, and heart condition. Most adults take between 0.125 mg and 0.25 mg once a day. Never change your dose on your own. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure the level of digoxin in your blood is in a safe range — not too high and not too low.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and remember within 12 hours, take it as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 12 hours since your missed dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one, as this can cause serious side effects.
storage: Store digoxin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the medication in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids, fiber supplements, or certain cholesterol medicines (like cholestyramine) at the same time as digoxin, as they can lower the amount of digoxin your body absorbs — ask your pharmacist about timing. Avoid starting or stopping any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements without talking to your doctor first. St. John's Wort can lower digoxin levels in your blood. Avoid a high-fiber diet change without telling your doctor. Limit alcohol and do not take over-the-counter medicines without checking with your pharmacist.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite; stomach pain or diarrhea; blurred, yellow, or green vision, or seeing halos around lights; confusion, dizziness, or feeling faint; fast, slow, or very irregular heartbeat; unusual weakness or tiredness; or swelling in your legs or feet that gets worse. These may be signs that your digoxin level is too high (digoxin toxicity), which can be dangerous.
when_it_works: Digoxin starts working within a few hours for slowing an irregular heartbeat. However, for heart failure, it may take several days to weeks before you notice you can breathe easier or have more energy. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better — digoxin controls your condition but does not cure it. Keep taking it as prescribed.
special_populations: Older adults: Digoxin is used with extra caution in older adults because kidneys work less well with age, which can cause digoxin to build up to dangerous levels. Lower doses are often needed and more frequent blood tests may be required. Kidney disease: If you have kidney problems, your dose will likely be lower. Tell your doctor about any kidney issues. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking digoxin if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: Digoxin can be used in children, but doses are very carefully calculated by weight — never give a child an adult dose.
